summary: A status report on the Internet Gateway developed by BBN as of September 1982, including message formats and gateway procedures. It is not an implementation specification. This RFC is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 823 describes the Internet gateway that BBN built for the DARPA Internet, as it stood in 1982. It explains how the machine checked and forwarded each datagram, how it asked its neighbours which networks they could reach, and what it measured and reported about its own operation. The document is a description of one implementation, not a standard.

how did the early internet gateways route traffic
subtitle: A status report on the router that ran the early Internet, and the protocols it used.

tldr.problem: By 1982 the Internet needed a router that could work as part of an operational communications service rather than a research testbed, and that could handle many networks, access control and monitoring.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes the BBN gateway: how it checks and forwards a datagram, the Gateway-to-Gateway Protocol it used to learn distances to networks from its neighbours, the monitoring and error reporting it ran, and how the software was split into a process per network plus shared gateway code.

sections.title: What This Document Is
sections.content:
The memo is a status report on the Internet gateway developed by BBN, describing it as of September 1982. It presents detailed descriptions of message formats and gateway procedures, but it is not an implementation specification, and such details are subject to change.

The gateway design was originally documented in IEN-30, Gateway Routing: An Implementation Specification, and later updated in IEN-109, How to Build a Gateway. The memo reflects changes made both in the Internet protocols and in the gateway design since those documents were released, and it supersedes both.

The gateway's primary purpose is to route Internet datagrams to their destination networks. The datagrams are generated and processed as described in RFC 791. The memo describes how the gateway forwards datagrams, the routing algorithm and protocol used to route them, and the software structure of the current gateway. The implementation is written in macro-11 assembly language and runs in the DEC PDP-11 or LSI-11 16-bit processor.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a report on one particular machine, written so that others can see how it worked. The gateway's job was to take datagrams from one network and pass them to another, and the memo describes that job in detail: what the machine checked, how it decided where to send things, and what the software looked like.

sections.title: How the Gateway Evolved
sections.content:
Early versions of gateway software were implemented using the BCPL language and the ELF operating system. That implementation evolved into one that used the MOS operating system for increased performance. In late 1981 an effort began to produce a totally new gateway implementation. The primary motivation was the need for a system oriented towards the requirements of an operational communications facility, rather than the research testbed environment associated with the BCPL implementation. It was also generally recognised that the complexity and buffering requirements of future gateway configurations were beyond the capabilities of the PDP-11/LSI-11 and BCPL architecture, so the new implementation had a second goal of producing a highly space-efficient implementation in order to provide space for buffers and for the extra mechanisms, such as monitoring, needed for an operational environment.

One result of recent research was the thesis that gateways should be viewed as elements of a gateway system, where the gateways act as a loosely-coupled packet-switching communications system. For reasons of maintainability and operability, it is easiest to build such a system in a homogeneous fashion where all gateways are under a single authority and control, as is the practice in other network implementations. In order to create a system architecture that permitted multiple sets of gateways, each set under single control but acting together to implement a composite single Internet system, new protocols needed to be developed, such as the Exterior Gateway Protocol.

The memo also anticipates further changes to introduce support for new capabilities, such as large numbers of networks, access control and other requirements proposed by the Internet research community. It represents a snapshot of the current implementation rather than a specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The first gateways were research machines written in a language of the era. The memo explains why a new one was built: the Internet was becoming an operational service, with monitoring and many networks attached, and the old machines were too small to hold the buffers and the code that required. The design idea that came out of this was that a set of gateways under one authority should act together as one system.

sections.title: Forwarding an Internet Datagram
sections.content:
A host that wants an IP datagram to reach a host on another network sends the datagram to a gateway, attaching to it a local network header containing the address of the gateway. On receipt, the gateway checks the local network header for errors and performs any action required by the host-to-network protocol, such as verifying the local network header checksum or generating a local network acknowledgment. If the header indicates that the message contains an Internet datagram, the datagram is passed to the Internet header check routine, and all other messages that do not pass these tests are discarded.

The Internet header check routine performs a number of validity tests: the proper IP version number, a valid IP header length of at least 20 bytes, a valid IP message length, a valid IP header checksum, and a non-zero time to live field. Datagrams that fail these tests are discarded, causing an HMP trap to be sent to the Internet Network Operations Center. The Internet destination address is then examined to see whether the datagram is addressed to the gateway itself, by comparing each of the gateway's Internet addresses, one for each network interface, against the destination address. If no match is found, the datagram is passed to the forwarding routine. If it is addressed to the gateway, the IP options are processed; the gateway supports NOP, End of Option List, Loose Source and Record Route and Strict Source and Record Route. The datagram is then processed according to the protocol in the IP header, and if the protocol is not supported the gateway replies with an ICMP error message and discards the datagram. The gateway does not support IP reassembly, so fragmented datagrams addressed to it are discarded.

The gateway must make a routing decision for every datagram to be forwarded, and the routing algorithm provides two things: the network interface to use and the destination address to put in the local network header. The gateway maintains a dynamic routing table with an entry for each reachable network, holding a network number and the address of the neighbour gateway on the shortest route, or an indication that the gateway is directly connected. A neighbour gateway is one that shares a common network with this gateway. The distance metric is the number of hops, a gateway being zero hops from its directly connected networks and one hop from a network reachable via one other gateway. The Gateway-to-Gateway Protocol is used to update the table.

The destination network address in the IP header is matched against the routing table. If no match is found, the gateway drops the datagram and sends an ICMP Destination Unreachable message to the IP source. If an entry is found, the neighbour gateway's network address becomes the local network destination address, except when the final destination network is one the gateway is directly connected to, in which case the destination address comes from the IP header. If the routing procedure decides the datagram is to be sent back out the same interface it was read in, this gateway is not on the shortest path, but the datagram is still forwarded to the next address chosen; and if the datagram is not using the IP Source Route Option and the IP source network is the same as the network of the next gateway, an ICMP Redirect is sent to the source host saying another gateway should be used.

After the routing decision the datagram goes to the fragmentation routine. If the next network has a maximum message size smaller than the datagram, the datagram is fragmented according to the algorithm in the Internet Protocol specification, with certain IP options copied into the header of all fragments and others appearing only in the first. If fragmentation is needed but the don't fragment bit is set, the datagram is discarded and an ICMP error message is sent to the source. The datagram or its fragments then go to a routine that rebuilds the Internet header, decrementing the time to live by one and recomputing the IP checksum, and the local network header is built, choosing the interface and the destination address. Finally the datagram is enqueued on an output queue for delivery towards its destination. A limit is enforced on the size of the output queue for each interface so that a slow network does not unfairly use up all of the gateway's buffers; if a datagram cannot be enqueued because of that limit, it is dropped and an HMP trap is sent to the operations centre.
sections.plainLanguage: Forwarding a datagram is a fixed sequence of steps. Check the local header, then check the IP header for a bad version, a short header, a bad length, a bad checksum or an expired time to live. Work out which interface and which neighbour to use. Split the datagram if the next network cannot carry it whole. Lower the time to live, fix the checksum, write the local header, and queue it. Along the way, the gateway answers back to the sender when something is wrong, using ICMP messages for unreachable destinations, redirects, and packets it could not forward.

sections.title: The Gateway-to-Gateway Protocol
sections.content:
The Gateway-to-Gateway Protocol, GGP, is used to determine connectivity to networks and neighbour gateways and to implement a dynamic, shortest-path routing algorithm. When a gateway starts running it assumes that all its neighbour gateways are down, that it is disconnected from the networks to which it is attached, and that the distance reported in routing updates from each neighbour to each network is infinity. The connection to a network is declared up if the gateway can send and receive Internet datagrams on its interface to it; the method is network-dependent, and on some networks the gateway polls with GGP network interface status messages to find out whether an interface is operational. Two rules apply to distances: if the gateway can send and receive traffic on an interface its distance to that network is zero, and if it cannot its distance is infinity.

Connectivity to neighbours uses a K out of N algorithm. Every 15 seconds the gateway sends GGP Echo messages to each of its neighbours, and the neighbours respond with GGP echo replies. If there is no reply to K out of N echo messages, currently K=3 and N=4, the neighbour is declared down; if a neighbour is down and J out of M echo replies are received, currently J=2 and M=4, the neighbour is declared up. The values of J, K, M, N and the interval are operational parameters.

Routing information is exchanged in routing update messages, reliably, using sequence numbers and a retransmission and acknowledgment scheme. For each neighbour the gateway remembers the receive sequence number R from the most recent routing update. On receipt, it subtracts R from the update's sequence number S. If the difference is zero or more the update is accepted, an acknowledgment carrying S is sent and R is replaced with S; if the difference is negative the update is rejected and a negative acknowledgment carrying R is sent. The gateway also has a send sequence number N for updates to all neighbours, incremented each time a new update is created. When an acknowledgment arrives, the acknowledged number A is subtracted from N; if the result is non-zero an old update is being acknowledged and the most recent update is retransmitted to that neighbour, and if it is zero the update has been acknowledged. A negative acknowledgment that makes the difference negative causes the send sequence number to be reset to A+1 and the update to be retransmitted to all neighbours, because the sequence numbers at all gateways must stay correct. Updates are retransmitted periodically until acknowledged and whenever the send sequence number changes, and are sent only to neighbours that are up.

A routing update contains a list of networks reachable through this gateway and the distance in hops to each. It contains a network only if the gateway believes it is as close or closer to that network than the neighbour that is to receive the update. The gateway keeps an N by K distance matrix, where N is the number of networks and K the number of neighbour gateways, with an entry dm(I,J) giving the distance to network I as reported by neighbour J, plus a vector of the connectivity to each neighbour. The minimum distance to network I is the minimum over all neighbours of the distance to that neighbour plus the distance the neighbour reports to network I; if the network is attached to the gateway and the gateway can send and receive traffic on its interface, that entry is set to zero. Using that minimum distance vector the gateway computes which neighbour to send traffic to for each network, and then works out the updates to send: it reports a network to a neighbour only if it is as close or closer than that neighbour, and the update carries the address of the network and the minimum distance to it. New updates are sent if one of the gateway's interfaces changes state, if one of its neighbours changes state, or if it receives an update from a neighbour different from the one it had received before.

A non-routing gateway forwards Internet traffic but does not implement the GGP routing algorithm. The networks behind it are known in advance to routing gateways and are considered directly connected to it. A routing gateway will forward a datagram to a non-routing gateway if it is addressed to a network behind it, but will always prefer another routing gateway at the same number of hops, using the non-routing path only when the routing gateway path is down.
sections.plainLanguage: The gateway learns the shape of the network from its neighbours. Every fifteen seconds it pings each of them; a neighbour that misses three of four pings is taken to be down, and one that answers two of four is taken to be up. Each neighbour reports the networks it can reach and how many hops away they are, and the gateway adds its own distance to that neighbour to work out the shortest route. The updates carry sequence numbers, so a neighbour can say which one it has, and updates are resent until they are acknowledged.

sections.title: Monitoring, Debugging and Error Reporting
sections.content:
Several protocols give the gateway its operational abilities. The Cross-Net Debugging Protocol is used to load the gateway and to examine and deposit data, with op-codes for NOP, Debug, End Debug, Deposit, Examine and Create Process. The Host Monitoring Protocol collects measurements and status information from the gateways; exceptional conditions are reported in HMP traps, and the status of a gateway's interfaces, neighbours and the networks it can reach is reported in the HMP status message.

Two types of gateway statistics are defined by HMP. The Host Traffic Matrix records the number of datagrams that pass through the gateway with a given IP source, destination and protocol number. The gateway throughput message collects counters that the gateway keeps: datagrams dropped because the destination network or host was unreachable; per interface, datagrams received with IP errors, datagrams received for the gateway itself, datagrams received to be forwarded, datagrams looped, bytes received, datagrams sent originating at the gateway, datagrams sent to destination hosts, datagrams dropped because of flow control limitations, datagrams dropped because of a full queue, and bytes sent; and per neighbour, routing updates sent to and received from, datagrams sent originating at the gateway, datagrams forwarded to, datagrams dropped because of flow control limitations, datagrams dropped because of a full queue, and bytes sent.

The gateway generates ICMP messages under the appropriate circumstances: Echo Reply, Destination Unreachable, Source Quench, Redirect, Time Exceeded, Parameter Problem and Information Reply.

The Exterior Gateway Protocol permits other gateways and gateway systems to pass routing information to the DARPA Internet gateways, so that a user can perceive all of the networks and gateways as part of one total Internet system even though the exterior gateways are disjoint and may use a different routing algorithm. Its important elements are neighbour acquisition, the procedure by which a gateway asks to become a neighbour of another and that other accepts or refuses; neighbour up and down, the procedure by which a gateway decides whether another is up; network reachability information, the facility used to pass routing and neighbour information between gateways; and gateway going down, the ability of a gateway to inform others that it is going down and has no routes left, so that it can go down in an orderly way without disrupting the rest of the system. A complete description is in IEN-209.
sections.plainLanguage: Besides forwarding, the machine reported on itself. A debugging protocol let an operator load it and look inside. The monitoring protocol sent periodic statistics about each interface and each neighbour, and raised traps when something went wrong, such as a queue filling up. ICMP messages told the sending host about unreachable destinations and about better gateways to use. And the exterior gateway protocol was the door to the rest of the Internet, letting gateways outside exchange routing information with these ones.

sections.title: The Gateway Software
sections.content:
The gateway runs under the MOS operating system, which provides multiple processes, interprocess communication, buffer management, asynchronous input and output, and a shareable real-time clock. There is a MOS process for each network the gateway is directly connected to. A data structure called a NETBLOCK holds the variables of interest for each network and pointers to local network routines; the network processes run common gateway code while network-specific functions are dispatched to the routines pointed to in the NETBLOCK. There are also processes for gateway functions that require their own timing, such as GGP and HMP.

The software divides into three parts: MOS device drivers, network software and shared gateway software. The device drivers handle sending and receiving data for each type of hardware interface, with routines for initialisation, initiation and interruption on both the transmit and receive sides. The supported devices are the ACC LSI-11 1822, the DEC IMP11a 1822, the ACC LHDH 1822, the ACC VDH11E, the ACC VDH11C, the Proteon Ring Network, the RSRE HDLC, Interlan Ethernet, BBN Fibernet, and two ACC XQ/CP devices, the X.25 and the HDH, which were planned but not yet supported.

For each connected network the gateway has a set of eight routines handling local network functions: Up.net performs local network initialisation such as flapping the 1822 ready line; Sg.net handles specific local network timing functions such as timing out 1822 destination deads; Rc.net is called when a message has been received and checks for input errors; Wc.net is called when a message has been transmitted and checks for output errors; Rs.net sets up a buffer or buffers to receive messages on the network interface; Ws.net transmits a message to the network interface; Hc.net checks the local network header of a received message and performs any local network protocol tasks; and Hb.net rebuilds the local network header. There are network routines for Arpanet, Satnet, the Proteon Ring Network, the Packet Radio Network, the Rsre HDLC Null Network, Ethernet, Fibernet and Telenet X.25, which was planned but not yet supported.

The shared gateway software performs the Internet processing of a datagram, including routines to check the IP header, perform IP fragmentation, calculate the IP checksum, forward a datagram, and implement the routing, monitoring and error reporting protocols. When the gateway starts, each network process calls its local network initialisation routine and read start routine, which sets up two maximum network size buffers for receiving datagrams, and then waits for an input complete signal from the network device driver. When a message arrives the operating system signals the appropriate network process, which wakes up and runs the net read complete routine. That routine is the major message processing loop, and it calls the local network read complete routine, starts more reads, checks the local network header, checks the Internet header, checks whether the datagram is for the gateway, forwards the datagram if necessary, and sends an ICMP error message if necessary.

The GGP process periodically sends GGP echoes to each of the gateway's neighbours to determine neighbour connectivity, sends interface status messages addressed to itself to determine network connectivity, and sends out routing updates when necessary. The HMP process handles timer-based gateway statistics collection and the periodic transmission of traps.
sections.plainLanguage: The machine ran one process per connected network, so a slow network could not hold up the others, and the common code that did the actual Internet work was shared between them. Each network type supplied eight small routines for its own quirks, such as reading its headers and waking it up, while everything to do with IP sat in the shared part. A separate process handled the routing protocol and another the monitoring.

viz.caption: THE STEPS IN FORWARDING ONE DATAGRAM

items.title: Input
items.text: Check the local network header and do whatever the host-to-network protocol requires.

items.title: IP header checks
items.text: Version, header length, message length, header checksum and time to live.

items.title: Routing
items.text: Match the destination network against the routing table to pick an interface and a neighbour.

items.title: Redirects
items.text: Tell the source host if another gateway would have been a shorter way.

items.title: Fragmentation
items.text: Split the datagram if the next network cannot carry it whole.

items.title: Header rebuild
items.text: Decrement the time to live, recompute the checksum and build the local header.

items.title: Output
items.text: Queue the datagram, and drop it with a trap if the queue is full.

viz.caption: THE GGP MESSAGE TYPES AND THEIR NUMBERS

items.label: Routing Update
items.desc: The networks reachable through this gateway and the distance to each.

items.label: Acknowledgment
items.desc: Confirms a routing update, carrying its sequence number.

items.label: Negative Acknowledgment
items.desc: Rejects a routing update and names the sequence number it expected.

items.label: GGP Echo
items.desc: Polling a neighbour to find out whether it is up.

items.label: GGP Echo Reply
items.desc: The neighbour's answer to an echo.

items.label: Network Interface Status
items.desc: Reports the state of one of the gateway's own interfaces.
